story.headline: A chip-led stock slump, with the Nasdaq down about 5%, knocked the Australian dollar 1% lower and lifted the yen and gold. The Bank of England raised rates to 4% and hinted at more.

reads.policy: The Bank of England raised rates and hinted at more, joining most big central banks that still lean toward higher rates. Fed officials kept arguing for a December hike, and European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde kept hers open without promising it. With these moves expected, currencies react to hints about the next step.
reads.growth: The US job market stays firm, with very few layoffs, and workers are producing more per hour, which lets firms grow without pushing up prices. German factories recovered part of a deep August slump. Friday's US and Canadian jobs figures are the next big read.
reads.inflation: Oil bounced back after new tanker attacks, so the energy push on prices has not gone away. In the US, falling labour costs per unit of output ease the risk that wages keep inflation high. The Bank of England now expects UK inflation to climb further next year, which is why it is still raising rates.
reads.risk: A sharp selloff in US chip and AI stocks turned markets fearful, wiping out the gains that followed Tuesday's election. Money went to the yen, gold and Treasury bonds, while the Australian and New Zealand dollars fell most. Whether this fear lasts is now a bigger driver than any single data release.
reads.tot: Oil climbed back after more tankers were hit near the Strait of Hormuz and hopes for a US–Iran deal faded. That raises the energy bill again for importers like Japan and the euro area and gives exporters like Canada a little more income. Today the stock slump mattered more to those currencies than oil did.
reads.positioning: Hedge funds hold their biggest bets against the Canadian dollar and also bet against the euro and the kiwi, while real money investors bet for the euro. Big bets on the yen and gold mean days like today, when both rose, reward the side that is already full. New figures arrive Friday afternoon.
reads.fiscal: Canada tabled its federal budget with tax breaks for business investment and money for energy projects; the full borrowing figures are still being checked. A Democratic Congress makes President Trump's spending plans harder to pass, which trims support for the dollar. France's debt worries still weigh on the euro.

fed.summary: The Federal Reserve held rates on October 28 with two officials voting to hike, and strong US figures have made a December hike look likely. Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack said Thursday rates still need to rise in small steps.
fed.why: US inflation is running well above the Fed's 2% goal on high energy prices, and layoffs remain rare, so the economy can take higher rates. Strong productivity growth is easing wage pressure.
fed.watch: The October jobs report at 7:30 AM CT Friday: strong hiring would all but lock in a December hike, while a weak one plus falling stocks could trim it.

boc.summary: The Bank of Canada raised rates to 2.50% in October, its first hike since 2023, and Governor Tiff Macklem told senators Thursday that more may be needed. He said the bank will move carefully, one meeting at a time.
boc.priced: December: another hike slightly more likely than not.
boc.why: Energy has lifted Canadian inflation, which the bank sees near 3.5% by year-end, but growth is running well below what it expected.
boc.watch: Canada's October jobs figures at 7:30 AM CT Friday and the details of the federal budget tabled Thursday; the bank's January outlook will reflect the budget.

rbnz.summary: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand surprised by holding at 2.75% in October, and weak job figures since have cut bets on a December hike. That leaves the kiwi with less support going into Saturday's election.
rbnz.priced: December: hike now slightly less likely than not.
rbnz.why: Inflation is still above the 1–3% target and the board agreed more tightening is likely, but unemployment has risen to its highest since 2015.
rbnz.watch: New Zealand's general election on Saturday and any comments from the bank before its December 9 decision.

ecb.summary: The European Central Bank held at 2.50% in October and pointed to a December hike. President Christine Lagarde said Thursday many figures will come in first, so a hike is likely but not promised.
ecb.why: Energy costs have pushed euro-area inflation to about double the 2% goal, though underlying prices are steadier, so the bank sees no reason to rush beyond one hike.
ecb.watch: Energy prices and euro-area business surveys before the December 17 decision.

boj.summary: The Bank of Japan held at 1.25% in October, and minutes of its September meeting show the board backs more rises. A December hike looks likely, which gives the yen extra support on top of its role as a safe place.
boj.why: The bank judges inflation to be running at its goal, with prices rising beyond energy, and one member has said the pace of hikes may need to quicken.
boj.watch: Governor Kazuo Ueda's speech at 10:00 AM CT Friday, Japanese wage figures, and any move by Tokyo to buy yen; the next decision is December 18.

rba.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised rates to 4.85% on November 3, the highest since 2008, but three of nine members wanted to wait. Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser said Thursday inflation is too high by any measure, yet markets still expect a pause.
rba.why: Inflation has run hotter than the bank expected and will stay above its target until late 2027, but a weakening job market argues for caution.
rba.watch: Australian jobs and inflation figures before the December 8 decision, and the global mood, which drove the Aussie lower Thursday.

boe.summary: The Bank of England raised rates to 4.00% on November 5, its first hike since 2023, with all nine members wanting a rise. Governor Andrew Bailey said it is unlikely to be the last while the Middle East conflict lasts.
boe.why: Energy is pushing UK inflation up, and the bank now expects it near 5% by the middle of next year, well above its 2% goal.
boe.watch: UK growth and jobs figures and oil prices before the December 17 decision; an end to the Iran conflict would weaken the case for another hike.

snb.summary: The Swiss National Bank holds its rate at zero, and Chairman Martin Schlegel said Thursday it can still sell francs if needed. Higher Swiss inflation makes another cut less likely, though not a hike.
snb.priced: December: markets split; no move is the slight favourite.
snb.why: Fuel lifted Swiss inflation to its highest since late 2023, but underlying prices stayed calm, so the bank has no reason to raise rates.
snb.watch: Swiss price figures and the franc's strength before the December 10 decision.

USD.summary: The dollar sits in the upper half of the board because the Federal Reserve is still expected to raise rates in December and US inflation runs hot. Democrats' win of both houses of Congress and a slump in US tech stocks weigh on it.

notes.policy: The Fed's next move still looks like a hike, likely in December, and very few layoffs back that up.
notes.inflation: US inflation is running well above the Fed's goal, mostly on fuel, though oil's sharp fall could start to ease it.
notes.fiscal: Democrats won both houses of Congress, so President Trump's spending plans look harder to pass, which takes some support from the dollar.

EUR.summary: The euro sits near the bottom of the board: growth is uneven, energy imports cost more, and France's debt worries weigh on it. A likely European Central Bank hike in December and a weaker US dollar give it some support.

notes.policy: The European Central Bank held in October and points to a hike in December, so it lags banks that are moving sooner.
notes.growth: Euro-area growth is uneven: France shrank over the summer, Italy stalled and business surveys keep missing.
notes.inflation: Euro-area inflation rose to 4.0% in October, mostly on energy, which keeps pressure on the European Central Bank to hike.
notes.tot: The euro area buys most of its energy abroad, so high oil drains money out of the region.
notes.positioning: Speculators hold their biggest bets against the euro in years, so good news could force them to buy it back.
notes.fiscal: Two of the three big rating firms now have France on negative outlook, which keeps investors wary of euro-area bonds.

GBP.summary: The pound tops the board: the Bank of England raised rates on November 5 and said it is unlikely to be the last, inflation is high and business surveys are strong.

notes.policy: The Bank of England raised rates to 4% on November 5, with all nine members in favour, and hinted at more.
notes.growth: UK business surveys have been stronger than expected, with factories at their busiest in two years, even though shoppers are gloomy.
notes.inflation: UK inflation rose to its highest in about a year, which keeps the Bank of England leaning toward hikes.
notes.positioning: Broad measures show speculators betting heavily against the pound, so a firm Bank of England could force them to buy it back.

JPY.summary: The yen sits low on the board because Japanese rates are far below other major economies' and high oil costs Japan money. It still gains when markets get scared, as it did when US chip stocks slumped on November 5.

notes.policy: The Bank of Japan's rate is still far below others', but minutes of its September meeting show the board backs more rises, pointing to a December hike.
notes.risk: The yen gains when investors look for safety, and it was the strongest major currency when US tech stocks slumped on November 5.
notes.tot: Japan imports almost all its energy, so high oil drains money out of the country.
notes.positioning: Broad measures show speculators holding unusually big bets on the yen, which could unwind fast if it weakens.

CHF.summary: The franc sits in the middle of the board: Swiss inflation is low, so the central bank has no reason to raise rates, but the franc still draws money when markets get nervous.

notes.inflation: Swiss inflation rose to 1.5% in October, mostly on fuel, but underlying prices are calm, so the Swiss National Bank still has no reason to raise rates.
notes.risk: The franc tends to gain when investors look for safety, though in the November 5 stock slump the yen and gold drew more of that money.

AUD.summary: The Aussie scores well because Australia's rates are now the highest among major economies and it sells resources abroad. But it falls hard when global markets get nervous, and its central bank has hinted at a pause.

notes.policy: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised rates to 4.85% on November 3, the highest of the major banks, but it dropped its hint of more.
notes.growth: Business surveys slipped into decline in October and unemployment is at a five-year high.
notes.inflation: Underlying inflation ran hotter than the bank expected and is set to stay high until late 2027.
notes.tot: Australia sells gas and metals abroad, and its trade surplus hit a seven-month high in September, bringing money into the country.
notes.positioning: Real money investors hold some of their biggest bets against the Aussie in years, so good news could force them to buy it back.

CAD.summary: The loonie scores well now that the Bank of Canada has started raising rates and oil still brings money in. Growth is the soft spot, and oil's sharp fall on hopes of an end to the Iran war trims its support.

notes.policy: The Bank of Canada raised rates in October and Governor Tiff Macklem says more may be needed, so a December hike is slightly more likely than not.
notes.growth: Canada's economy did not grow in July or August, well short of what the Bank of Canada expected.
notes.inflation: Producer and raw-material prices are rising fast, which keeps the Bank of Canada leaning toward more hikes.
notes.tot: Canada is a big oil exporter, so crude brings money in, though oil is well below last week's highs as hopes of an end to the Iran war come and go.

NZD.summary: The kiwi sits in the middle of the board: New Zealand's central bank held rates when markets expected a hike, and unemployment has risen to its highest since 2015. Firm dairy prices limit the damage, and Saturday's election adds uncertainty.

notes.growth: Unemployment rose to 5.7%, the highest since 2015, and jobs fell, which weakens the case for a December rate hike.
notes.tot: Dairy prices, New Zealand's biggest export, have risen at three auctions in a row, bringing money into the country.
notes.positioning: Speculators are betting heavily against the kiwi, so good news could force them to buy it back.
